/Issued 132 AM MST Sun Nov 1 2026/ 

 - Meteorological Overview:

A moist southwesterly flow aloft continues to overrun a cooler 
and nearly saturated air mass at the surface. This has maintained 
an abundance of low clouds, while waves of light rain showers move
northward through the forecast area. Surface temperatures have 
risen well above freezing for most locations, so freezing drizzle 
or light freezing rain hasn't been much of a problem tonight; 
however, there is some stubborn colder air at the surface north of
the Hi-Line, mainly over northern Hill and Blaine counties, where
there maybe some isolated instances of freezing drizzle through 
the morning hours. Also, some colder air is slowly seeping 
southeastward over the plains along the Rocky Mountain Front. 
Fortunately, these areas are mainly seeing fog rather than falling
precipitation. Speaking of fog, the aforementioned light 
precipitation delayed the onset of fog development over much of 
central and north-central MT tonight, but the fog looks to begin 
expanding over the area heading towards the early dawn hours. 
Also, dense fog has developed over the Gallatin Valley and looks 
to expand to other southwest valleys as the night progresses.

The Pacific NW trough responsible for the moist southwesterly 
flow ejects eastward towards the Northern Rockies and sends waves 
of more widespread precipitation through the forecast area today 
through Monday morning. This system will be undergoing weakening 
and shearing as it approaches and its colder air aloft is not 
scheduled to arrive until tonight into Monday morning. So snow 
levels will be over 7000 ft for most locations, generally yielding
liquid precipitation at and below pass level. The one exception 
to this will be along the Continental Divide where spotty light 
snow will fall before tonight.

H700 temperatures finally fall to around -5C late night into 
early Monday and this will bring more efficient accumulating snow,
heaviest over the Madison/Gallatin ranges above 6000 ft. There 
will be a brief period with snow levels falling to the 
valley/plains floors Monday morning, although it does not appear 
that this will be long enough to support widespread accumulating 
snow impacts. Northwesterly winds may also get gusty later 
tonight, though gusts look to stay below 40 mph and the strongest 
winds should quickly move east of the forecast area Monday 
morning. Ensembles continue to favor ridging aloft to bring milder
and drier conditions for much of the upcoming workweek; however, 
a weak system may move through around Wednesday and bring a few 
isolated showers to the southwest and along the Continental 
Divide. Forecast uncertainty increases towards the end of the 
workweek, but most ensembles highlight zonal troughs bringing 
breezy to windy conditions and mostly mountain precipitation 
heading into next weekend. - RCG

 - Forecast Confidence & Scenarios:

...Areas of dense fog through the morning hours...

The fog has been most widespread over the plains west of I15 so 
far tonight, but will begin to expand to other areas of central 
and north-central MT with light shower activity diminishing and 
ending. Also the southwestern valleys have also been observing 
patchy dense fog development, which looks to expand in coverage 
prior to the arrival of the more widespread precipitation later 
this morning. Impacts will mostly be directly related from the 
reduced visibility, but frost deposition or even some freezing 
drizzle may cause some slippery spots to develop on roadways, 
especially the bridges and elevated surfaces. These roadway 
impacts will generally be confined to plains locations along and 
west of I15. The dense fog advisory covering much of 
central/north-central MT was left as is and some southwest valleys
were added to the advisory, including the Bozeman, Dillon, and 
Helena areas. 

...Light mountain snow and lower elevation rain and snow Sunday 
through Monday morning...

The main trough swings through today through early Monday and 
brings a wave of widespread precipitation to much of the forecast 
area. Aside from some light snow along the Continental Divide and 
perhaps some spotty freezing drizzle over the plains west of I15, 
most of the precipitation will be falling in the form of rain 
until the colder air aloft moves in tonight. The overall pattern 
and NBM probabilities continue to favor elevations over 6000 ft in
the Madison and Gallatin ranges for the best chance (60 to 80%) 
of snowfall amounts in excess of 3 inches. Lighter snows, 
generally up to a couple inches, look to fall along the 
Continental Divide and the central island ranges. The colder air 
is still not looking to be optimally aligned with the moisture for
lower elevation snows, even in the Gallatin Valley where
